svg.aria-label: Diagram: Amazon EC2 now provides five types of status checks: system, instance, attached EBS, application, and performance. Status checks are performed every minute, returning a pass or a fail status, and if one or more checks fail the overall status of the instance is impaired. System, instance, attached EBS and performance checks are managed by Amazon EC2 and cannot be disabled or deleted, while application status checks are opt-in and monitor HTTP or HTTPS responses and can be suppressed during deployments. System, instance and attached EBS checks run on every instance, the attached EBS metric is available only for Nitro instances, and performance status checks run only on supported accelerated instance types. The new performance status check monitors for hardware issues that impact accelerated computing instance performance without making the instance unreachable, and these issues do not require scheduled maintenance, which is a condition the previous model could not express: an instance that passes every check while doing less work than you are paying for. The documented example is a GPU memory error that can require an instance reboot to reset the GPU and trigger row remapping, resolving the issue without replacing the instance. The PerformanceStatus object returned by DescribeInstanceStatus includes Status, ImpairedSince and Remediation fields, and when Status is impaired the Remediation field carries the recommended action such as reboot, neither of which is available through the metric. The critical interaction is that a failed performance status check increments the StatusCheckFailed_Performance metric and also increments the aggregate StatusCheckFailed metric, so any existing alarm watching the aggregate, including automatic instance recovery and Auto Scaling health replacement, now fires on a nonterminal condition whose documented remediation is a reboot rather than a replacement, trading a short reboot for a scarce-capacity relaunch on accelerated instances. Alongside the check, EC2 Detailed Monitoring adds OpenTelemetry metric support, one-minute GPU metrics, and a 10-second CPU utilization metric intended for sizing and scaling with EC2 Auto Scaling, all opt-in through categories applied across a fleet and incurring standard CloudWatch Detailed Monitoring charges, while the performance status checks themselves are free and available in all commercial Regions and GovCloud US.
svg.title: A fifth status check, feeding the aggregate metric your automation already watches
svg.text: A state the old model could not express: running, reachable, and slower.
“hardware issues that impact accelerated computing instance performance without making the instance
unreachable. These issues do not require scheduled maintenance.”
Five checks now — most mental models stop at two
system AWS’s infrastructure · “require AWS involvement to repair”
instance your OS and network · “require your involvement”
attached EBS volume I/O · Nitro instances only
application HTTP/HTTPS · opt-in, suppressible during deploys
performance degraded but working · accelerated types only
The line that changes an alarm you wrote years ago
“A failed performance status check also increments the StatusCheckFailed metric.”
Auto-recovery alarms. Auto Scaling health replacement. Dashboards. Runbook triggers. None were written
with degradation in mind, because it did not exist as a signal.
On a GPU fleet that trades a 60-second reboot for a scarce-capacity relaunch — and discards AWS’s own fix.
THE FIELD THAT TELLS YOU WHAT TO DO
PerformanceStatus.Status
PerformanceStatus.ImpairedSince
PerformanceStatus.Remediation → reboot
From DescribeInstanceStatus. Not from the metric.
THE DOCUMENTED REPAIR
“a GPU memory error can require an instance reboot
to reset the GPU and trigger row remapping, which
resolves the issue without replacing the instance.”
Nobody’s instinct at 3am. Write it down first.
Shipped alongside, opt-in by fleet category
OpenTelemetry metrics · one-minute GPU metrics · a 10-second CPU metric for EC2 Auto Scaling, which
finally matches the resolution a high-resolution alarm can evaluate at. Standard Detailed Monitoring charges.
The aggregate is a good human signal and a poor machine one: it unions conditions with incompatible remedies.
Alarm per metric for automation. And when a GPU job slows down, check instance status before re-profiling the model.
